title: Beef Olives
subtitle: Stuffed braising steak rolls in a rich brown gravy
excerpt: Thin slices of braising steak wrapped around a herby breadcrumb stuffing, then braised low and slow in beef stock. A proper old-fashioned British supper that needs very little attention once it is in the pot.
sourceNotes: Traditional British braised beef roll dish, long associated with Scotland and the North of England, adapted from classic household cookery sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely and freeze in the braising liquid. Defrost overnight and reheat gently on the hob until piping hot.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch easily in a large casserole. The rolls keep well for three days in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make a day ahead and reheat slowly. The flavour deepens overnight.

content.text: Beef olives are not olives at all. They are neat rolls of thinly beaten braising steak around a savoury stuffing, cooked in gravy until tender. The rolls must be tied firmly so they hold their shape throughout the long braise.

items.prepNote: cut into 4 thin slices, beaten flat

content.text: Melt the butter in the frying pan over a medium heat. Soften the onion and bacon for 5 minutes. Tip into a bowl and leave to cool for 10 minutes.
Add the breadcrumbs, parsley, thyme, beaten egg, salt and pepper to the bowl. Mix well until the stuffing holds together loosely.
Lay each slice of beef flat. Divide the stuffing between the four slices. Roll each one up tightly and tie in two places with kitchen twine.
Dust the rolls in plain flour. Heat the oil in the frying pan over a high heat. Brown the rolls on all sides for about 4 minutes total. Set them aside.
Pour the beef stock and Worcestershire sauce into the large saucepan. Bring to a simmer.
Add the browned rolls to the stock. Cover with a lid and cook on a very low heat for 90 minutes, turning the rolls halfway through.
Lift the rolls out carefully. Remove the twine. Taste the braising liquid and season. Pour it over the rolls to serve.

items.symptom: The rolls come apart during cooking.
items.cause: The twine was not tied tightly enough, or the rolls were disturbed too often.
items.fix: Tie the rolls in two spots and avoid moving them during the first hour of braising.

items.symptom: The gravy is very thin at the end.
items.cause: The heat was too high and the stock reduced too fast, or no flour was used on the rolls.
items.fix: Remove the rolls, bring the gravy to a brisk boil for 5 minutes to reduce and thicken.

items.symptom: The beef is tough after 90 minutes.
items.cause: The heat was too low or the slice was too thick.
items.fix: Cover and continue cooking for another 30 minutes on a very gentle simmer.
